answer_text: The boiling point of water depends on the surrounding pressure: at sea level the atmospheric pressure is about 101 kPa, so water must be heated to 100 °C before its vapor pressure equals the external pressure and it can boil. At high altitude the atmospheric pressure is lower, so water’s vapor pressure matches the ambient pressure at a lower temperature, causing it to boil at a temperature below 100 °C.

At high altitude the atmospheric pressure is lower, so water molecules need less energy to escape the liquid phase. Because the boiling point is defined as the temperature at which the vapor pressure of water equals the surrounding pressure, that temperature is lower when the surrounding pressure is reduced. Consequently, water boils at a lower temperature on a mountain than at sea level.
